text:
Ibn al-Baitar's scope — the largest pre-modern pharmacopoeia

The Compendium of Simple Medicaments and Foods — the largest pharmaceutical encyclopedia in Islamic history. Ibn al-Baitar (1197–1248) travelled extensively across North Africa, Spain, Syria, and Egypt collecting plants personally — a field approach anticipating modern pharmacognosy. His compendium documents 1,400 plants, 300 of which are not in any earlier Arabic source. He critically evaluated earlier sources (Ibn Sina, Dioscorides, Al-Razi) and corrected numerous errors. The work supersedes the Canon of Medicine in raw botanical scope and represents the peak of classical Arabic pharmacobotany.

Original: كتاب الجامع لمفردات الأدوية والأغذية — أكبر موسوعة دوائية في التاريخ الإسلامي
title: Ibn al-Baitar's scope — the largest pre-modern pharmacopoeia

text:
Al-Qinnab — the most detailed early cannabis pharmacology

Cannabis — the drink made from it intoxicates and maddens; eating it in the required amount promotes urination. Ibn al-Baitar's cannabis entry is the most detailed pre-modern pharmacological documentation — distinguishing: the psychoactive dose (intoxicating, maddening) from the therapeutic dose (diuretic), the seed from the leaf and flower, and internal from external applications. He notes the difference between hemp seed (used nutritionally and medicinally) and the flowering tops (psychoactive). This precision of dose-effect documentation is unusual in medieval pharmacology.

Original: القنب — الشراب المعمول منه يسكّر ويجنّن، والأكل منه بقدر الحاجة يُدرّ البول
title: Al-Qinnab — the most detailed early cannabis pharmacology

text:
Henna — Ibn al-Baitar's expanded documentation

Henna — it consolidates wounds, prevents inflammation, and strengthens the hair. Ibn al-Baitar significantly expands the Canon of Medicine's henna entry — adding the hair-strengthening application not mentioned by Ibn Sina, and documenting specific preparations for different conditions: the paste for wounds, the leaf decoction for hair, the seed oil for skin. The lawsone compound in henna has documented antifungal activity (validated for hair/scalp applications) and antimicrobial wound activity.

Original: الحناء — تلحم الجروح وتمنع الالتهاب وتقوي الشعر
title: Henna — Ibn al-Baitar's expanded documentation

text:
Sabbara (Aloe) — connecting Eastern and Western documentation

Sabbara (aloe): it heals sores and consolidates fresh wounds. The best quality is clear and yellow in color. Ibn al-Baitar's aloe entry notes the quality distinction between good and poor aloe latex — the clear yellow indicating high aloin content (pharmacologically active laxative compounds). He connects the wound-healing properties to the gel rather than the latex. The Arabic documentation of aloe extends its presence in the archive from Cobo's colonial Andean documentation (MMA-091) to Unani medicine, completing a chain from Egyptian medicine (Ebers Papyrus) through Greek/Roman, Unani, and Andean traditions.

Original: الصبر — يشفي القروح ويلحم الجروح الطازجة. أجوده ما كان صافياً أصفر اللون
title: Sabbara (Aloe) — connecting Eastern and Western documentation

text:
Zaafaran — the most valued Arabic medicine

Saffron — among the most excellent and beneficial medicines for the heart; it gladdens the soul and strengthens the heart and liver. Ibn al-Baitar's saffron entry extends the existing archive documentation (MMA-028) by adding specific dosage information (one mithqal per day maximum) and the warning against excessive use ('produces heaviness of the head'). The cardiac and mood applications are consistent across Egyptian, Ayurvedic, Persian, Unani (Ibn Sina), and now Ibn al-Baitar documentation — five independent Islamic-era or Islamic-adjacent traditions.

Original: الزعفران — من أجود الأدوية وأنفعها للقلب، يُفرّح النفس ويقوي القلب والكبد
title: Zaafaran — the most valued Arabic medicine

text:
Habbatus Sawda — expanded documentation

Black seed (Nigella sativa) — it opens obstructions, strengthens the stomach, and heals internal sores. Ibn al-Baitar's black seed entry is longer than Ibn Sina's — documenting 15 separate therapeutic applications. He specifically records its use for gastric ulcers ('heals internal sores') — now validated by thymoquinone's documented anti-ulcer activity through prostaglandin-sparing mechanisms. The entry also documents black seed for respiratory conditions, consistent with modern research showing bronchodilatory effects.

Original: الحبة السوداء — تفتح السدد وتقوي المعدة وتشفي القروح الباطنية
title: Habbatus Sawda — expanded documentation

text:
Ibn al-Baitar's 300 new plants — undocumented species

Ibn al-Baitar documented approximately 300 plants not previously described in the pharmacological literature — primarily plants from the Iberian Peninsula (Al-Andalus), the Maghreb (North Africa), and sub-Saharan plants known through trans-Saharan trade. These include endemic Iberian plants that were never incorporated into the mainstream European pharmacopoeia despite their documented medicinal use by Arabic-speaking physicians in Spain. The loss of this botanical knowledge during the Reconquista represents one of the greatest undocumented pharmacological losses in history. Key plants include specific Andalusian lavender varieties, endemic Iberian Cistus species, and Atlas Mountain medicinal plants.

Original: [Al-Baitar documents approximately 300 plants not found in earlier Arabic or Greek sources]
title: Ibn al-Baitar's 300 new plants — undocumented species

text:
Definition of medicine and the four humours

Medicine is the science by which we learn the various states of the human body in health and when not in health, and the means by which health is likely to be lost and, when lost, is likely to be restored. Ibn Sina opens the Canon with a definition that positions medicine as a science, not a craft — a radical assertion in 1025 CE. The four humours (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) are presented not as metaphysical entities but as physiological categories with observable properties and pharmacological implications. This framework, inherited from Galen but systematized by Ibn Sina, was the basis of both Islamic and European medicine for 600 years.

Original: الطب علم يتعرف منه أحوال بدن الإنسان من جهة ما يصح ويزول عنه الصحة
title: Definition of medicine and the four humours

text:
Kitab al-Adwiya al-Mufrada — simple drugs and their classification

Simple drugs are those that act by their complete substance. Book II of the Canon — the Materia Medica — is Ibn Sina's pharmacological masterwork. It classifies 760 plants, minerals, and animal products by their primary qualities (hot/cold, moist/dry on a four-degree scale) and their specific actions. The degree system is a genuine attempt at pharmacological quantification — a drug that is 'hot in the third degree' produces stronger effects than one 'hot in the first degree.' This system of graduated pharmacological intensity has no parallel in any earlier medical tradition.

Original: الأدوية المفردة هي التي تفعل فعلها بتمام جوهرها
title: Kitab al-Adwiya al-Mufrada — simple drugs and their classification

text:
Sana (Senna) — the canonical laxative

Senna: hot and dry in the second degree. It purges yellow bile and black bile. Ibn Sina documents senna as the primary oral laxative — distinguishing it from more violent purgatives by its moderate degree of action. The preparation: senna leaves steeped in hot water with violet and tamarind to moderate its griping action. This specific preparation — senna + tamarind to reduce cramping — is still the standard pharmaceutical formulation of senna today, 1,000 years later.

Preparation: Senna leaves steeped in hot water with tamarind and violet; drunk fasting
Indication: Constipation, melancholy (black bile excess), bilious conditions

Original: السنا: حار يابس في الدرجة الثانية. ينقي الصفراء والسوداء.
title: Sana (Senna) — the canonical laxative

text:
Afyun (Opium) — pain and sleep

Opium: cold and dry in the fourth degree. It numbs the senses and quiets pain. Ibn Sina's documentation of opium is the most sophisticated in any pre-modern medical tradition. He distinguishes: (1) the lethal dose from the therapeutic dose, (2) the use for acute pain from chronic use leading to habituation, (3) topical from internal application. He specifically warns that opium 'should be given in small quantities and with great caution' — the first documented pharmacological warning about opioid dependency in medical literature.

Preparation: Small amounts dissolved in wine for internal pain; applied in oil for local analgesia
Indication: Severe pain, insomnia, cough, diarrhea — with explicit warning about habituation

Original: الأفيون: بارد يابس في الدرجة الرابعة. مخدّر للحواس، مسكّن للأوجاع.
title: Afyun (Opium) — pain and sleep

text:
Irsa (Licorice root) — the Canon's harmonizer

Licorice root: moderate in heat and cold, moist in the first degree. It benefits the chest and lungs. Ibn Sina's documentation of licorice adds the sixth independent tradition to this plant's convergence record — Egyptian, Greek/Roman, Persian/Zoroastrian, Ayurvedic, Chinese, and now Unani. The Canon specifically recommends licorice for respiratory conditions, cough, and as a demulcent — consistent with glycyrrhizin's documented anti-inflammatory and soothing properties. Ibn Sina also documents licorice as an antidote to bitter medicines, explaining its near-universal use as a flavoring agent in compound preparations.

Preparation: Decoction in water; combined with bitter medicines as sweetener and harmonizer
Indication: Cough, respiratory infections, chest complaints, thirst, antidote to bitter medicines

Original: عرق السوس: معتدل الحرارة والبرودة، رطب في الأولى. ينفع الصدر والرئة.
title: Irsa (Licorice root) — the Canon's harmonizer

text:
Qinnab (Cannabis) — pain, appetite, and the mind

Cannabis: hot and dry in the third degree. It dries out the moisture of the brain. Ibn Sina documents cannabis for: ear pain (oil dropped into the ear), wound cleaning, and brain conditions. He is the first physician to document cannabis-induced tachycardia ('it quickens the heart') — an observation that precedes modern understanding of cannabis's cardiovascular effects by nearly a thousand years. His warning that excess cannabis 'corrupts the mind' and produces 'flatulent colic' is among the earliest documented descriptions of adverse cannabis effects.

Preparation: Seed oil dropped into ear for pain; seeds applied to wounds; smoke inhaled (with warnings)
Indication: Ear pain, wound cleaning, brain moisture excess, pain

Original: القنب: حار يابس في الدرجة الثالثة. يجفف رطوبات الدماغ.
title: Qinnab (Cannabis) — pain, appetite, and the mind

text:
Kafur (Camphor) — the cooling agent

Camphor: cold and dry in the third degree. It suppresses sexual desire. Ibn Sina documents camphor as the primary cooling medicine — used for fever, inflammatory conditions, and as an antiseptic. The observation that camphor suppresses sexual desire is consistent with modern research showing camphor at high doses has anti-androgenic effects. Ibn Sina also documents camphor as an insect repellent — consistent with modern understanding of camphor's insecticidal properties — and as a preservative, explaining its use in embalming.

Preparation: Applied in oil to skin for fever and inflammation; used in compound preparations
Indication: Fever, inflammatory conditions, insect repellent, wound antiseptic

Original: الكافور: بارد يابس في الدرجة الثالثة. يقطع الشهوة.
title: Kafur (Camphor) — the cooling agent

text:
Zaafaran (Saffron) — heart and mood medicine

Saffron: hot and moist in the second degree. It gladdens the soul and strengthens the heart. Ibn Sina's documentation of saffron for cardiac and mood conditions directly validates the existing archive entry (MMA-028). The Canon documents saffron as a primary cardiac tonic and antidepressant — 1,000 years before modern RCTs confirmed saffron's antidepressant activity comparable to fluoxetine (Prozac). The Canon also warns that excessive saffron produces 'immoderate laughter' — possibly the earliest documented description of saffron's psychoactive effects at high doses.

Preparation: Infused in warm water or wine; taken with honey
Indication: Depression, heart palpitations, cardiac weakness, insomnia

Original: الزعفران: حار رطب في الدرجة الثانية. يفرّح النفس ويقوي القلب.
title: Zaafaran (Saffron) — heart and mood medicine

text:
Kurkum (Turmeric) — liver and wound medicine

Turmeric: hot and dry in the second degree. It benefits the liver and gallbladder. Ibn Sina documents turmeric for liver conditions, wound healing, and as a blood purifier — connecting the Canon documentation to the existing archive entry for turmeric (MMA-012) which includes Ayurvedic and other tradition entries. The Canon's documentation of turmeric for liver conditions is consistent with curcumin's documented hepatoprotective activity. Ibn Sina also recommends turmeric applied topically for wounds — consistent with curcumin's antimicrobial and wound-healing properties.

Preparation: Powder in warm water; applied topically in oil for wounds
Indication: Liver conditions, jaundice, wound healing, blood purification

Original: الكركم: حار يابس في الدرجة الثانية. ينفع الكبد والمرارة.
title: Kurkum (Turmeric) — liver and wound medicine

text:
Ward (Rose) — the universal healer

Rose: cold and moist in the first degree. It strengthens the principal organs. Ibn Sina's documentation of rose water is extraordinary in its scope — he documents it for: cardiac strengthening, eye inflammation, headache, mouth and throat inflammation, intestinal conditions, and as a general tonic. Rose water became the universal solvent of Unani compound preparations. The Canon's documentation of rose for cardiac and eye conditions connects to the Egyptian, Greek/Roman, and Persian documentation of rose for the same indications.

Preparation: Rose water as solvent for compound preparations; rose oil applied topically; rose petals in decoction
Indication: Cardiac weakness, eye inflammation, headache, mouth inflammation, digestive conditions

Original: الورد: بارد رطب في الأولى. يقوي الأعضاء الرئيسية.
title: Ward (Rose) — the universal healer

text:
Azadiracht — the bitter purifier

Neem (azadiracht): hot and dry in the second degree. It expels worms. Ibn Sina documents neem for intestinal parasites and skin conditions — converging with the Ayurvedic documentation of neem (nimba) in the Charaka Samhita for the identical antiparasitic and skin disease applications. This cross-tradition convergence between Unani and Ayurvedic documentation for the same plant and same indication is among the strongest dual-system validations in the archive.

Preparation: Bark decoction for internal parasites; leaves applied topically for skin conditions
Indication: Intestinal parasites, skin diseases, fever

Original: أزدرخت: حار يابس في الثانية. طارد للديدان.
title: Azadiracht — the bitter purifier

text:
Zanjabil (Ginger) — the warming digestive

Ginger: hot and dry in the third degree. It improves digestion and strengthens sexual vitality. Ibn Sina documents ginger for digestive conditions, as an aphrodisiac, and for cold-type joint pain — the same applications documented in Greek/Roman, Ayurvedic, and Chinese traditions. The Canon is particularly detailed on ginger's use for digestive weakness — recommending it before meals to 'prepare' the stomach. This application is consistent with gingerol's documented effect on gastric motility.

Preparation: Fresh or dried root in hot water; combined with honey; added to food
Indication: Digestive weakness, nausea, cold-type arthritis, sexual debility

Original: الزنجبيل: حار يابس في الثالثة. يحسّن الهضم ويقوي الباه.
title: Zanjabil (Ginger) — the warming digestive

text:
Kammun (Cumin) — digestive and anti-flatulent

Cumin: hot and dry in the second degree. It expels wind. Ibn Sina documents cumin as the primary carminative — for flatulence, digestive pain, and as a flavoring in medicinal preparations. The Canon distinguishes between Persian cumin (Bunium persicum) and common cumin (Cuminum cyminum), noting that Persian cumin is more effective medicinally. This botanical distinction — identifying a pharmacologically superior variety within the same species complex — demonstrates the empirical precision of the Canon's pharmacobotany.

Preparation: Seed decoction; ground in preparations; added to food as medicinal spice
Indication: Flatulence, digestive pain, colic, general digestive weakness

Original: الكمون: حار يابس في الثانية. يطرد الرياح.
title: Kammun (Cumin) — digestive and anti-flatulent

text:
Kundur (Frankincense) — inflammation and wounds

Frankincense: hot and dry in the second degree. It dries sores and consolidates wounds. Ibn Sina's documentation of frankincense (Boswellia) for wound healing and inflammatory conditions extends the convergence signal for MMA-075 (Frankincense/Boswellia) to include Unani as a fifth tradition. The Canon specifically recommends burning frankincense for respiratory conditions — consistent with the Kyphi (Egyptian) documentation and modern research on incensole acetate's psychoactive and anti-inflammatory effects.

Preparation: Resin applied to wounds; burned for respiratory; dissolved in oil
Indication: Wound healing, respiratory conditions, inflammatory conditions

Original: الكندر: حار يابس في الثانية. يجفف القروح ويلحم الجروح.
title: Kundur (Frankincense) — inflammation and wounds

text:
Rawand (Rhubarb) — liver and purgative

Rhubarb: hot and dry in the second degree. It strengthens the liver and stomach. Ibn Sina documents rhubarb root for liver conditions and as a moderate purgative — extending the convergence signal for rhubarb (already in the archive as Kampo's Daio/MMA-030 and Chinese Bencaojing's Dahuang) to include Unani as a fourth tradition. The Canon's documentation of rhubarb for liver conditions specifically connects to the anthraquinone mechanism — anthraquinones stimulate bile production (choleretic activity) which validates the liver-strengthening traditional claim.

Preparation: Root powder in warm water; combined with other herbs in compound preparations
Indication: Liver weakness, constipation, digestive conditions, jaundice

Original: الراوند: حار يابس في الثانية. يقوي الكبد والمعدة.
title: Rawand (Rhubarb) — liver and purgative

text:
Habbatus Sawda (Black Seed/Nigella) — the prophetic medicine

Black seed: hot and dry in the third degree. It benefits every condition except death. Ibn Sina documents Nigella sativa (black seed / black cumin) with the prophetic hadith — the statement attributed to the Prophet Muhammad that black seed cures everything except death. The Canon documents it for: respiratory conditions, digestive complaints, skin conditions, and as a general tonic. This is one of the most extensively studied traditional plants in modern Islamic medicine research, with documented anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, and immunomodulatory activity from thymoquinone.

Preparation: Seeds ground and taken in honey; oil pressed and applied topically; seeds added to food
Indication: Respiratory conditions, digestive complaints, skin conditions, general immunity

Original: الحبة السوداء: حارة يابسة في الثالثة. تنفع من كل داء إلا الموت.
title: Habbatus Sawda (Black Seed/Nigella) — the prophetic medicine

text:
Rumman (Pomegranate) — the sixth tradition

Pomegranate: cold and moist in the first degree. It strengthens the stomach and prevents diarrhea. Ibn Sina's documentation of pomegranate adds Unani as the sixth independent tradition documenting pomegranate medicinally — alongside Egyptian, Greek/Roman, Persian/Zoroastrian, Tibetan, and Ayurvedic documentation already in the archive. The Canon recommends pomegranate rind specifically for antiparasitic applications — converging with Dioscorides' documentation of the root bark for the same indication.

Preparation: Fruit eaten; rind decocted for antiparasitic; juice drunk
Indication: Digestive complaints, intestinal parasites, diarrhea, stomach weakness

Original: الرمان: بارد رطب في الأولى. يقوي المعدة ويمنع الإسهال.
title: Rumman (Pomegranate) — the sixth tradition

text:
Hinna (Henna) — skin and wound medicine

Henna: cold and dry in the second degree. It consolidates wounds and prevents inflammation. Ibn Sina documents henna (Lawsonia inermis) for wound healing, inflammatory skin conditions, and headache (applied to the forehead). This is the primary medicinal documentation of henna in classical literature — while henna's cosmetic use is universal, its pharmaceutical use for wound healing documented by Ibn Sina is consistent with lawsone's (henna's active compound) documented antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory properties.

Preparation: Paste applied to wounds and inflamed skin; paste applied to forehead for headache
Indication: Wound healing, inflammatory skin conditions, headache, burns

Original: الحناء: بارد يابس في الثانية. يلحم الجروح ويمنع الالتهاب.
title: Hinna (Henna) — skin and wound medicine

text:
Hummayat — the fever chapters

Fever is in itself a disease or the symptom of a disease, and everything that is a fever has a cycle. Ibn Sina's fever classification is the most sophisticated in any pre-modern medical tradition: he distinguishes ephemeral fever (from fatigue, emotion), humoral fevers (corresponding to each of the four humours), and putrid fevers (from rotting matter in the organs). The recognition that malarial fevers follow a three-day cycle (Plasmodium vivax) or four-day cycle (P. malariae) — documented in detail in the Canon — is a genuine epidemiological observation that predates germ theory by 850 years.

Original: الحمى في نفسها مرض أو عرض مرض وكل ما هو حمى فله دورة.
title: Hummayat — the fever chapters

text:
Sirsam — meningitis and brain inflammation

Sirsam: a hot inflammation in the brain or its membranes [meningitis]. Ibn Sina's description of sirsam is the first systematic description of meningitis in world medical literature — he distinguishes it from other brain conditions by the specific symptoms of neck rigidity, photophobia, and altered consciousness. The treatment: cooling medicines applied to the head, reduction of brain heat, and opium for pain and sleep. The observation that neck rigidity distinguishes sirsam from other fevers (Kernig's sign precursor) demonstrates clinical observation of extraordinary precision.

Original: السرسام: ورم حار في دماغ أو أغشيته.
title: Sirsam — meningitis and brain inflammation

text:
Tiyaqat — theriac and compound antidotes

The Great Theriac: a grand compound of sixty drugs or more. Ibn Sina documents the Theriac — the legendary universal antidote inherited from the Greek tradition (Mithridates VI, Galen) — with 60+ ingredients including opium, viper flesh, and dozens of plant medicines. The Canon's documentation of theriac is historically significant because Ibn Sina attempts to rationalize it pharmacologically — explaining each ingredient by its humoral action — rather than simply transmitting it as magical tradition. Theriac remained in use as a pharmaceutical preparation in European and Islamic medicine until the 18th century.

Original: الترياق الكبير: مركب عظيم من ستين دواءً أو أكثر.
title: Tiyaqat — theriac and compound antidotes

text:
Convergence note — Licorice: six traditions confirmed

With Ibn Sina's Canon documentation, licorice root (Glycyrrhiza species) is now confirmed in six independent medical traditions: Egyptian Ebers Papyrus (c.1550 BCE), Greek/Roman Dioscorides (77 CE), Persian/Zoroastrian texts, Ayurvedic Charaka Samhita (yashtimadhu), Chinese Shennong Bencaojing (gancao), and now Unani Canon of Medicine (irsa). Six independent civilizations across four continents documented the same plant genus for overlapping indications across 2,600 years. This is the single strongest convergence signal in the entire archive — and glycyrrhizin's documented anti-inflammatory and antiviral activity (used in Japan as an approved anti-hepatitis drug) provides the pharmacological validation.

Original: [Cross-archive analysis]
title: Convergence note — Licorice: six traditions confirmed

text:
Anees (Anise) — Drug Monograph from Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine

PLANTACOPIA ENTRY — ANEES (ANISE)

Arabic Name: أَنِيسُون (Anīsūn); also rendered Anees or Anyson in Arabic-Islamicate sources. The term is a direct Arabicisation of the Greek ἄνισον (anison).

Modern Identification: Pimpinella anisum L. (family Apiaceae). Confidence: HIGH.

Synonyms and Cross-References: Known to Dioscorides (Materia Medica, Book III, ch. 56) as anison; cited by Galen (De Simplicium Medicamentorum Temperamentis, Book VII) who affirms its heating and drying action. Ibn Sina integrates both Greek authorities and the Persian pharmacological tradition [hikmat-i Yunani and Persian naturalist observation] into his account.

---
MIZAJ (TEMPERAMENT / KRASIS)
---
Quality: Hot and Dry.
Degree: Hot in the Second Degree [darajah al-thaniyah]; Dry in the First to Second Degree [bayna al-ula wa-l-thaniyah].
Ibn Sina notes that the green (fresh) herb is somewhat more moist than the dried seed, and that Syrian-grown anise is considered superior in potency to Egyptian varieties, being more aromatic and pungent. The seed [bazr al-anīsūn] is the principal medicinal part.

---
KHAWAS (SPECIFIC PROPERTIES / VIRTUES)
---
1. Mufattih [aperient/opening]: Opens obstructions of the liver, spleen, kidneys, and urinary passages.
2. Mulattif [subtilising/attenuating]: Refines and rarefies thick, viscous humours.
3. Musakkin [analgesic/sedating]: Alleviates colic pain and intestinal griping.
4. Mudir al-bawl [diuretic]: Promotes the flow of urine.
5. Mudir al-hayd [emmenagogue]: Stimulates menstrual flow when suppressed.
6. Mudir al-laban [galactagogue]: Increases the production of breast milk in nursing women.
7. Kasir al-riyah [carminative]: Disperses flatulence and intestinal gas.
8. Muqawwi al-mida [stomachic]: Strengthens and warms the stomach.
9. Munawwim [soporific/mild sedative]: In certain preparations and dosages, promotes sleep.
10. Muqawwi al-bah [aphrodisiac]: Ibn Sina states it mildly strengthens sexual potency when consumed consistently.
11. Taskheen al-badan [general warming]: Produces a gentle systemic warmth useful in cold-dominant [barid] constitutions.

---
MANAFI (THERAPEUTIC INDICATIONS / BENEFITS)
---
Gastrointestinal:
— Relieves flatulence, bloating, and intestinal colic [qulanj].
— Useful in nausea and hiccough [fawwaq] arising from cold or windy causes.
— Strengthens a weak or cold stomach [mida baridah].
— Aids digestion of heavy foods.
— Effective against diarrhoea of cold humoral origin.

Urinary and Reproductive:
— Promotes urination; beneficial in urinary retention [ihtibaas al-bawl] and gravel [hasah] of the kidneys and bladder.
— Stimulates suppressed menstruation [ihtibaas al-hayd] when the cause is cold obstruction.
— Increases milk production in nursing mothers.

Respiratory:
— Eases difficulty of breathing [usr al-nafas] and asthma [rabu] of cold-phlegmatic origin.
— Assists in expelling thick phlegmatic mucus from the lungs and bronchi.

Neurological and General:
— Anise seed, applied as a poultice or smelled, relieves headache arising from cold or flatulent causes.
— Ibn Sina cites Dioscorides in affirming that sleeping with anise near the face promotes restful sleep and prevents nightmares [kawabis].
— Beneficial for epilepsy [sara] of phlegmatic origin in children, administered in small doses.
— Strengthens eyesight [muqawwi al-basar] when used in collyria [kuhl] preparations.

Topical / External:
— Anise oil [duhn al-anīsūn] rubbed onto the abdomen relieves colic.
— Applied to the chest, it warms and opens the lung passages.
— As a fumigant [bukhur], it repels vermin and insects.

---
MAZARR (HARMS / CONTRAINDICATIONS)
---
— Excessive use may overheat the blood and produce bilious [safrawi] imbalances, particularly in persons of hot, sanguine temperament [mizaj damawi].
— Contraindicated or to be used with caution in summer and in hot climates.
— May cause headache if used in excess by those with hot temperaments.
— Prolonged use may excessively dry the body in persons already of dry constitution [mizaj yabis].

---
ISLAAH (CORRECTIONS / AMENDMENTS)
---
To correct its excessive dryness: combine with honey [asal] or sweet oils to buffer its desiccating action.
To temper its heat in sensitive patients: combine with rose water [ma al-ward] or dilute in cold water before administration.
For bilious temperaments, pair with cooling, moistening agents such as purslane [baqlah] or cucumber seed [bazr al-qitta].

---
BADAL (SUBSTITUTES)
---
Ibn Sina notes the following may substitute for anise when it is unavailable:
1. Fennel seed [bazr al-shamar / razyanaj] — closest substitute; similar temperament and carminative action.
2. Caraway [karwiya] — acceptable substitute for flatulence and digestive indications.
3. Cumin [kammun] — acceptable substitute for colic and diuretic indications, though hotter and more drying.
Note: Substitution ratios follow the classical rule: use equal weight of fennel; slightly less caraway (approx. three-quarters) due to its stronger action.

---
DOSAGE
---
Seed (dried, powdered): 1 to 3 mithqals [approx. 4.5 to 13.5 grams] per dose, taken with warm water or honey water.
Decoction: Boil 2–4 mithqals of seed in water; strain and drink warm.
Oil (expressed or distilled): A few drops on a cloth applied to the abdomen; or 3–5 drops in warm water.
As an emmenagogue or diuretic: Best taken in the morning on an empty stomach in warm water.
For children (e.g., in colic or epilepsy): Reduce dose proportionally; typically one-quarter to one-third of adult dose depending on age and constitution.

---
COMPOUND PREPARATIONS (MURAKKABAT) CITED
---
1. Jullanjubin with anise [jullanjubin al-anīsūn]: Anise seed macerated in oxymel [sirka wa-asal] — used for liver obstructions and urinary complaints.
2. Anise–fennel decoction: Combined equal parts anise and fennel seed, decocted, used for respiratory phlegm and flatulence.
3. Anise electuary [ma'jun]: Anise seed ground with honey and ginger [zanjabil] — used as a stomachic and aphrodisiac.
4. Eye salve [kuhl]: Anise ash [ramad al-anīsūn] mixed with antimony [kohl al-ithmid] — mentioned in the context of strengthening weak eyes.
5. Sleep-promoting pillow infusion: Anise tied in cloth and placed near the head during sleep — cited by Ibn Sina with reference to Dioscorides.

---
CROSS-REFERENCES TO EARLIER AUTHORITIES
---
— Dioscorides (Pedanius Dioscorides, 1st century CE): Cited for anise's diuretic, galactagogue, and soporific properties, and for the custom of sleeping beside anise to encourage restful sleep and prevent nightmares. Ibn Sina endorses these observations.
— Galen (Claudius Galenus, 2nd century CE): Cited for the classification of anise as hot and dry in the second degree, and for its action as a subtiliser [mulattif] of thick humours; Ibn Sina refines Galen's account by distinguishing between seed and herb.
— Persian tradition: Ibn Sina notes that Persian physicians [hukama al-Furs] particularly valued anise in colic remedies and as a children's medicine for gas and griping, reflecting pre-Islamic Persian pharmacopoeial usage absorbed into the Islamicate synthesis.
